value.overview: The Zone-tailed Hawk is a dark, medium-sized raptor of the Americas. Its bold white tail bands and pale bars across the flight feathers are most visible when it soars. The species often resembles a Turkey Vulture in shape, flight style, and behavior, a resemblance that may help it approach prey unnoticed. It occupies forested mountains, canyons, dry woodland, foothills, and other rugged landscapes from the southwestern United States through Central America and much of South America.
value.classification: The Zone-tailed Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Buteo. Its scientific name is Buteo albonotatus.
value.identification: Adults are mostly black or very dark brown, with silvery-white barring on the flight feathers and several broad white bands across the tail. The wings are long and narrow, and the bird commonly soars with the wings held in a shallow dihedral, rocking from side to side. The cere and feet are yellow, and a small pale area may show in front of the eye. Juveniles have more finely barred tails and less distinct wing markings. It is easily confused with Turkey Vulture and Common Black Hawk.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America to South America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon but regularly recorded native hawk, listed as both resident and migratory. It occurs in several regions, including the northwest, Caribbean lowlands, foothills, and mountain landscapes, and has been recorded on both slopes. Breeding has been reported in northwestern Costa Rica, although the species is generally local and much less numerous than many migrant raptors. It favors forest edges, wooded valleys, dry forest, canyons, and open areas near forest.
value.migrationStatus: Zone-tailed Hawks are short-distance migrants in the northern part of their range and mostly resident farther south. In Costa Rica, the species is considered both resident and migratory: some birds remain year-round, while others pass through or move seasonally. Records may increase during raptor migration periods, but it is not one of Costa Rica’s most abundant migrant hawks.
value.breeding: The Zone-tailed Hawk usually nests in trees or on cliff ledges in rugged, relatively undisturbed terrain. The nest is a large stick platform lined with softer material, and the same territory or nest area may be used repeatedly. The female generally lays one to three eggs, and both adults participate in rearing the young. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported in the northwest, but detailed information on nesting dates, productivity, and the full breeding distribution remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of small and medium-sized birds, mammals, reptiles, and amphibians. Depending on location, prey may include passerines, woodpeckers, quail, lizards, snakes, frogs, and small mammals. It commonly hunts from soaring flight or a concealed perch, then drops or glides toward prey. The hawk may associate with Turkey Vultures while searching for food, using a similar flight silhouette to reduce detection by potential prey.
value.behavior: This hawk is often seen soaring high above forested hills, canyons, and valleys, especially where rising air currents allow it to travel with little effort. Its flight is distinctive: the wings are held in a slight V and the bird frequently rocks from side to side. It is usually solitary or seen in pairs, though several may gather during migration or over favorable thermal currents. Vocalizations are generally less noticeable than its aerial behavior.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category. Trend information is limited in parts of Central and South America.
